Participation is unrelated to incentives.
An increase in participation proves the subsidy had no effect.
The subsidy changed too, creating a competing explanation.
42983.feedback: Two relevant conditions changed together. Without further evidence their contributions cannot be separated.

42985.q: A behavioral intervention was tested only on volunteers from one workplace. Which statement accurately describes the evidence?
options: It proves effectiveness in every workplace.
It provides evidence about that sample; broader effectiveness needs additional support.
It supplies no evidence because volunteers are never informative.
It establishes the intervention’s mechanism solely from the sample size.
42985.feedback: A restricted sample can be informative while limiting generalization to other settings.

42989.q: Two studies estimate an intervention effect at 4 and 5 percentage points, each with an uncertainty interval from −2 to 10. Does the one-point difference establish conflicting effects?
options: Yes; any different point estimates establish different underlying effects.
No; the estimates are close relative to their reported uncertainty.
Yes; overlapping intervals prove opposite mechanisms.
No; the true effect is necessarily exactly 4.5 points.
42989.feedback: Sampling variation can produce nearby estimates. Their uncertainty does not support treating the one-point difference as a demonstrated conflict.

42991.q: A trial finds that a default raises participation by 20 points among new employees. A firm plans to apply the same estimate to long-serving workers who already made active choices. What limitation matters?
options: Random assignment guarantees an identical effect in every population.
Prior choices make the trial’s result mathematically impossible.
A 20-point effect means participation must double in every group.
The trial identifies an effect for its participants; transfer to a group with prior active choices requires evidence.
42991.feedback: Internal evidence from one group does not guarantee the same response in a different decision context.

42993.q: Several small studies report a large behavioral effect, while a well-designed large replication reports a smaller positive effect. Which conclusion best combines magnitude and replication evidence?
options: Any smaller effect proves the underlying mechanism does not exist.
The evidence may support a positive effect while weakening the claim that it is as large as first reported.
A positive effect in the replication confirms the original magnitude exactly.
The number of small studies alone makes sample size and design irrelevant.
42993.feedback: Replicating a direction does not establish the original magnitude. Assessing both size and uncertainty can support a more modest conclusion.

43001.q: A person values avoiding a $20 loss more strongly than obtaining a $20 gain relative to the same reference point. Which pattern is illustrated?
options: Risk neutrality
Loss aversion
Availability from a vivid recent event
Perfectly symmetric valuation of gains and losses
43001.feedback: The comparison holds the amount fixed and shows greater weight on a loss relative to the reference point.

43003.q: After seeing a vivid news report of a rare accident, a traveler raises its estimated frequency without new statistical data. What is the availability-based explanation?
options: The report mechanically changes the true accident rate.
The traveler computes the rate from a larger random sample.
The traveler values losses and gains symmetrically.
Ease of recalling the event substitutes for evidence about its frequency.
43003.feedback: Salient, easy-to-recall examples can receive excessive weight when judging frequency.

43005.q: Two identical outcomes are framed as keeping $80 of an endowed $100 or losing $20 of it. A decision changes with the framing. Which explanation is consistent with this evidence, without claiming it is uniquely proven?
options: The frames produce different final wealth by definition.
Reference-dependent evaluation can make the loss frame more salient despite identical final wealth.
The change proves the person has different income in the two descriptions.
The frames eliminate any role for a reference point.
43005.feedback: The monetary outcome is the same. A difference in response is consistent with framing and reference dependence, though it alone does not uniquely identify a mechanism.

43007.q: A vivid report raises perceived accident risk, while a large representative dataset shows that the rate has not changed. Which response most directly corrects an availability-based inference?
options: Increase the estimated frequency further because the story is memorable.
Ignore both the story and the dataset because no probability can be estimated.
Treat the single report as more representative than the large dataset.
Use the representative frequency data while distinguishing vividness from prevalence.
43007.feedback: Representative base-rate evidence addresses frequency; vividness alone does not show a change in that frequency.

43009.q: A person rejects a fair gamble. Why does that fact alone not establish loss aversion?
options: Loss aversion requires accepting every fair gamble.
Ordinary risk aversion can also explain rejection; evidence about gains and losses around a reference point is needed.
Risk aversion and loss aversion are identical definitions.
Rejecting a gamble proves probability judgments are accurate.
43009.feedback: Risk aversion concerns curvature over outcomes; loss aversion concerns asymmetric valuation of gains and losses relative to a reference point. A single rejection need not distinguish them.

43011.q: After a recent burglary, residents become more worried. Local data also show a sustained increase in burglaries. Why is increased concern alone insufficient to diagnose availability bias?
options: A recent event prevents any rational response.
Availability bias requires no memorable events.
Statistical evidence cannot influence perceived risk.
The concern could reflect the documented increase in risk as well as the vivid event.
43011.feedback: A changed belief is not automatically a bias when relevant risk evidence also changes. The two explanations require discrimination.

43015.q: Two groups see the same accident-rate table; one also sees a vivid anecdote. Random assignment yields higher risk estimates only in the anecdote group. What does this design add?
options: It proves the true accident rate rose in the anecdote group.
It changes the table’s sample size for one group.
It establishes loss aversion rather than a judgment effect.
It isolates the anecdote’s effect while holding the statistical information fixed.
43015.feedback: Holding the table constant and randomly varying the anecdote supports an effect of salience on risk judgment.

43017.q: A policy analyst predicts that a $50 rebate framed as avoiding a loss will work identically for people who expected the rebate and people who did not. What does reference dependence suggest?
options: Equal dollars force identical reference points.
Different expectations may create different reference points, so equal dollars need not produce equal responses.
Only the final dollar amount can matter in a reference-dependent model.
A reference point changes the legal value of the currency.
43017.feedback: Expectations can affect whether an outcome is experienced as a gain or avoidance of a loss, limiting the prediction of identical responses.

43025.q: A voting rule ranks A above B. Voters’ individual comparisons of A with B stay fixed, but changing their views about C makes the social ranking put B above A. Which condition is violated?
options: The requirement that voters have no preferences
Independence of irrelevant alternatives
A rule requiring equal incomes
The arithmetic of vote totals only
43025.feedback: IIA requires the social comparison of A and B to depend on individual comparisons of that pair, not changed views about a third option.

43029.q: A rule violates independence of irrelevant alternatives in one example. Does that alone imply that every voter’s ranking is cyclic?
options: Yes; IIA is the definition of individual transitivity.
No; the collective rule can violate IIA even when each individual ranking is transitive.
Yes; adding an alternative necessarily changes every pairwise preference.
No; IIA places no restriction on a social ranking rule.
43029.feedback: IIA concerns how a collective pairwise ranking responds to preference profiles; it is distinct from consistency of each individual’s ranking.

43033.q: A designer claims that Arrow’s theorem proves no useful election rule can exist. Which correction best states the limitation of that claim?
options: The theorem guarantees all voting rules satisfy every fairness condition.
The theorem concerns satisfying a specified set of conditions together; a rule can remain useful while relaxing a condition.
The theorem applies only when there are exactly two alternatives.
The theorem says individual preferences cannot be transitive.
43033.feedback: An impossibility result about jointly meeting conditions is not a claim that every rule is useless. Practical design involves which conditions to retain or relax.

43039.q: Three equal-sized groups rank A>B>C, B>C>A and C>A>B. Which option wins a pairwise contest between A and B?
options: B by two groups to one
A unanimously
They tie
A by two groups to one
43039.feedback: The first and third groups prefer A to B; only the second prefers B.

43043.q: Three equal-sized groups rank A>B>C, B>C>A and C>A>B. Under sequential pairwise voting with sincere votes, compare agenda 1 (A versus B, then the winner versus C) with agenda 2 (B versus C, then the winner versus A).
options: Both agendas select A.
Agenda 1 selects B; agenda 2 selects C.
Both agendas select C.
Agenda 1 selects C; agenda 2 selects A.
43043.feedback: A beats B but then loses to C. B beats C but then loses to A. The cycle makes the final result depend on the agenda.

43050.q: Five voters have single-peaked preferences over one spending level, with ideal points 1, 3, 4, 8 and 10. Which level is the median ideal point and defeats any alternative in pairwise majority voting under these assumptions?
43050.feedback: The ordered middle ideal point is 4, not the mean 5.2. Single-peakedness makes the median proposal a majority winner.

43054.q: A median-voter prediction was derived for single-peaked preferences on one policy dimension. The election then adds a second independent policy dimension. What conclusion is warranted?
options: The arithmetic median on the first dimension must still win every multidimensional comparison.
Adding a dimension guarantees unanimous agreement.
The original theorem’s assumptions no longer suffice to guarantee a median policy winner.
All individual preferences must become cyclic.
43054.feedback: The one-dimensional ordering supports the median-voter result. Moving to multiple dimensions removes that guarantee without proving that a cycle must occur.

P62F-PC-LB-033.q: A price-taking firm faces a temporary output cap of 40 units. At 40 units, ATC is at its minimum of $12 and MC is $12; market price is $18. There are no externalities. If the cap is removed, rising MC reaches $18 at 70 units, where ATC exceeds its minimum. Which comparison correctly evaluates the two outputs?
options: At 40 units production is both productively and allocatively efficient; at 70 units it is neither.
At 40 units production is neither productively nor allocatively efficient; at 70 units it is both.
At 40 units production is productively efficient but not allocatively efficient; at 70 units it is allocatively efficient but not productively efficient.
At 40 units production is allocatively efficient but not productively efficient; at 70 units it is productively efficient but not allocatively efficient.
P62F-PC-LB-033.feedback: Minimum ATC establishes productive efficiency at 40. However, P exceeds MC there, so additional output has marginal value above marginal cost. Removing the cap permits P=MC at 70, establishing allocative efficiency even though ATC is above its minimum.

P62G-MON-L-091.q: Refer to the graph. If a regulator required the firm to operate at the D = MC outcome, which result follows from the displayed values?
options: Q rises to 60, P falls to $30, and the firm earns zero economic profit.
Q stays at 36, P falls to $30, and the firm earns positive economic profit.
Q rises to 60, P falls to $30, and the firm earns positive economic profit.
Q rises to 60, P stays at $42, and the firm earns positive economic profit.
P62G-MON-L-091.feedback: At Q=60 the demand and MC curves meet at $30. ATC is below $30 at that output, so (P−ATC)Q is positive. The regulated outcome expands output and lowers price while leaving positive economic profit.

P62B-ELAS-L-084.q: A product initially has few close substitutes. A 10% price increase reduces its quantity demanded by 4%. Later, several close substitutes become available; the same 10% price increase reduces quantity demanded by 16%. The comparison uses the same adjustment period, and income, tastes and the product’s necessity status are unchanged. A manager claims the larger response is merely a movement along demand and provides no evidence that responsiveness changed. Which evaluation is strongest?
options: Accept the claim: the ratios 0.4 and 1.6 describe movements along demand. Because the product itself is unchanged, responsiveness should be treated as constant despite the difference between those ratios.

Reject the claim: elasticity rises from 0.4 to 1.6 as close substitutes expand. Each price experiment moves along its own demand curve, while the comparison shows changed responsiveness across periods.
Reject the claim: elasticity rises from 0.4 to 1.6 because consumers have more time to adjust later. Equal experiment lengths do not constrain the time-horizon explanation for the larger response.

Reject the claim: elasticity rises from 0.4 to 1.6 because the product becomes more like a luxury. A larger observed response establishes changed necessity status despite the stated comparison controls.
P62B-ELAS-L-084.feedback: Using the stated percentage responses, |Ed| changes from 4/10=0.4 to 16/10=1.6. Each price change causes movement along the demand curve applicable then. The different responsiveness across periods is consistent with the new substitutes; equal adjustment periods and unchanged necessity status rule out the other explanations.

P62C-CPS-H-026.q: A firm earns $500 in revenue. Its explicit variable costs are $280 and its explicit fixed lease cost is $70. The owner also forgoes $40 of income from another job. What is accounting profit, and why is the forgone income treated that way?
options: $110; accounting profit subtracts explicit costs and the $40 forgone income.
$220; accounting profit excludes both the fixed lease and the $40 forgone income.
$190; accounting profit subtracts the lease but adds the $40 forgone income.
$150; accounting profit subtracts explicit costs, so the $40 forgone income is excluded.
P62C-CPS-H-026.feedback: Accounting profit is revenue minus explicit costs: $500−$280−$70=$150. The forgone $40 is an implicit opportunity cost used in economic profit, not an additional explicit cost.

P62E-COP-EL-011.q: A firm has standard U-shaped ATC. Initially MC crosses ATC from below at Q=80, where both equal $32. An annual license fee then rises, increasing fixed cost by $720 without changing variable cost. At Q=80, which comparison is correct, and what happens to the output that minimizes ATC?
options: ATC and MC both rise to $41; the ATC-minimizing output stays at 80.
ATC rises to $41 while MC stays $32; the new ATC-minimizing output is less than 80.
ATC rises to $41 while MC stays $32; the new ATC-minimizing output is greater than 80.
ATC stays $32 while MC rises to $41; the new ATC-minimizing output is greater than 80.
P62E-COP-EL-011.feedback: At 80 units the added fixed cost raises ATC by $720/80=$9, while MC is unchanged. MC is now below ATC, so expanding output lowers ATC; with the stated U-shaped curves, the minimum occurs at a larger output.

P62B-ELAS-L-059.q: A tax raises a drink’s price by 10% and reduces its quantity demanded by 18%, measured over the same period with other demand determinants held constant. Buyers switch to untaxed close substitutes. Which conclusion best connects the measured response to tax design?
options: Demand is elastic over the observed change (|Ed|=1.8); covering the close substitutes could reduce this substitution channel, but would not by itself determine the new tax revenue.
Demand is inelastic over the observed change (|Ed|=0.56); covering the close substitutes would necessarily lower tax revenue.
Demand is elastic over the observed change (|Ed|=1.8); changing the statutory payer would remove the substitution channel.
Demand is elastic over the observed change (|Ed|=1.8); covering the close substitutes would guarantee that quantity and tax revenue stay unchanged.
P62B-ELAS-L-059.feedback: The stated quantity response divided by the price change is 18/10=1.8. Untaxed close substitutes offer an avoidance margin. Expanding coverage can limit that margin, but revenue still depends on the tax rate and remaining quantity response.

P62C-CPS-LB-002.q: 6 buyers each want one unit with values [26, 32, 38, 44, 50, 56]; 6 sellers each can supply one with resource costs [49, 41, 57, 45, 53, 61]. Values and costs are in dollars. A 2-unit allocation uses the cheapest 2 sellers but serves the lowest-value buyer instead of the marginal buyer among the highest 2 values. A reassignment would restore the highest-value allocation without changing output, using $27 of real administrative resources. Which comparison is correct?
options: Reassignment recovers $20 before administration; its net change is $-7, because the existing allocation creates no surplus.
Reassignment leaves surplus unchanged before administration; its net change is −$27, because quantity does not change.
Reassignment recovers $24 before administration; its net change is $51, because administrative resources add to social gains.
Reassignment recovers $24 before administration; its net change is −$3, so retain the current allocation under these costs.
P62C-CPS-LB-002.feedback: The efficient allocation yields $20. Replacing the marginal served buyer valued at $50 with the lowest-valued buyer at $26 loses $24, leaving $-4. Correcting allocation restores $24, but costs $27, for a net change of $-3.

P62C-CPS-B3-008.q: A price ceiling raises consumer surplus by a net $22 before search costs, reduces producer surplus by $34, and creates $3 of real search costs not included in either surplus figure. What is the change in total surplus?
P62C-CPS-B3-008.feedback: Add the net consumer-surplus change to the producer-surplus change and subtract the separately stated real search cost: $22−$34−$3=−$15. A transfer component alone would not measure the full consumer-surplus change.

P62E-COP-LB-003.q: At Northstar Bakery, 3 workers each earn $120 per production period, and total fixed cost is $240 per period. The last worker raises output from 20 to 34 units; labor is the only variable input. A recurring fixed fee adds $240 per period and pay rises $15 per worker. Output, employment and productivity remain unchanged. Which new cost values are correct? Round final results to cents.
P62E-COP-LB-003.feedback: The new fixed cost is $480 and the wage bill is 3×$135=$405. Divide each by 34 for AFC and AVC; ATC uses their unrounded sum. The last worker adds 14 units, so MC=$135/14=$9.64.

P62E-COP-LB-006.q: At Ironwood Furniture, 4 workers each earn $135 per production period, and total fixed cost is $300 per period. The last worker raises output from 29 to 41 units; labor is the only variable input. A recurring fixed fee adds $240 per period and pay rises $15 per worker. Output, employment and productivity remain unchanged. Which new cost values are correct? Round final results to cents.
P62E-COP-LB-006.feedback: The new fixed cost is $540 and the wage bill is 4×$150=$600. Divide each by 41 for AFC and AVC; ATC uses their unrounded sum. The last worker adds 12 units, so MC=$150/12=$12.50.

P62E-COP-LB-009.q: At Harbor Roasters, 5 workers each earn $105 per production period, and total fixed cost is $180 per period. The last worker raises output from 47 to 56 units; labor is the only variable input. A recurring fixed fee adds $240 per period and pay rises $15 per worker. Output, employment and productivity remain unchanged. Which new cost values are correct? Round final results to cents.
P62E-COP-LB-009.feedback: The new fixed cost is $420 and the wage bill is 5×$120=$600. Divide each by 56 for AFC and AVC; ATC uses their unrounded sum. The last worker adds 9 units, so MC=$120/9=$13.33.

P62E-COP-LB-012.q: At Cedar Trail Bikes, 6 workers each earn $150 per production period, and total fixed cost is $420 per period. The last worker raises output from 54 to 60 units; labor is the only variable input. A recurring fixed fee adds $240 per period and pay rises $15 per worker. Output, employment and productivity remain unchanged. Which new cost values are correct? Round final results to cents.
P62E-COP-LB-012.feedback: The new fixed cost is $660 and the wage bill is 6×$165=$990. Divide each by 60 for AFC and AVC; ATC uses their unrounded sum. The last worker adds 6 units, so MC=$165/6=$27.50.

P62E-COP-LB-015.q: At Blue Peak Printing, 3 workers each earn $110 per production period, and total fixed cost is $210 per period. The last worker raises output from 18 to 31 units; labor is the only variable input. A recurring fixed fee adds $240 per period and pay rises $15 per worker. Output, employment and productivity remain unchanged. Which new cost values are correct? Round final results to cents.
P62E-COP-LB-015.feedback: The new fixed cost is $450 and the wage bill is 3×$125=$375. Divide each by 31 for AFC and AVC; ATC uses their unrounded sum. The last worker adds 13 units, so MC=$125/13=$9.62.

P62E-COP-LB-018.q: At Riverbend Textiles, 4 workers each earn $140 per production period, and total fixed cost is $360 per period. The last worker raises output from 40 to 53 units; labor is the only variable input. A recurring fixed fee adds $240 per period and pay rises $15 per worker. Output, employment and productivity remain unchanged. Which new cost values are correct? Round final results to cents.
P62E-COP-LB-018.feedback: The new fixed cost is $600 and the wage bill is 4×$155=$620. Divide each by 53 for AFC and AVC; ATC uses their unrounded sum. The last worker adds 13 units, so MC=$155/13=$11.92.

P62E-COP-LB-021.q: At Juniper Foods, 5 workers each earn $125 per production period, and total fixed cost is $270 per period. The last worker raises output from 44 to 54 units; labor is the only variable input. A recurring fixed fee adds $240 per period and pay rises $15 per worker. Output, employment and productivity remain unchanged. Which new cost values are correct? Round final results to cents.
P62E-COP-LB-021.feedback: The new fixed cost is $510 and the wage bill is 5×$140=$700. Divide each by 54 for AFC and AVC; ATC uses their unrounded sum. The last worker adds 10 units, so MC=$140/10=$14.00.

P62E-COP-LB-024.q: At Summit Glassworks, 6 workers each earn $160 per production period, and total fixed cost is $480 per period. The last worker raises output from 69 to 79 units; labor is the only variable input. A recurring fixed fee adds $240 per period and pay rises $15 per worker. Output, employment and productivity remain unchanged. Which new cost values are correct? Round final results to cents.
P62E-COP-LB-024.feedback: The new fixed cost is $720 and the wage bill is 6×$175=$1050. Divide each by 79 for AFC and AVC; ATC uses their unrounded sum. The last worker adds 10 units, so MC=$175/10=$17.50.

P62E-COP-LB-027.q: At Maple Street Media, 3 workers each earn $100 per production period, and total fixed cost is $195 per period. The last worker raises output from 15 to 26 units; labor is the only variable input. A recurring fixed fee adds $240 per period and pay rises $15 per worker. Output, employment and productivity remain unchanged. Which new cost values are correct? Round final results to cents.
P62E-COP-LB-027.feedback: The new fixed cost is $435 and the wage bill is 3×$115=$345. Divide each by 26 for AFC and AVC; ATC uses their unrounded sum. The last worker adds 11 units, so MC=$115/11=$10.45.

P62E-COP-LB-030.q: At Granite Toolworks, 4 workers each earn $145 per production period, and total fixed cost is $390 per period. The last worker raises output from 39 to 52 units; labor is the only variable input. A recurring fixed fee adds $240 per period and pay rises $15 per worker. Output, employment and productivity remain unchanged. Which new cost values are correct? Round final results to cents.

P62I-OLI-L-072.q: Two rival cruise lines keep fares at $72 and sell 30 units each in the kinked-demand model shown. Rivals match fare cuts but do not match fare increases. A per-unit cost increase raises this firm’s constant MC from $48 to $54, with demand and fixed cost unchanged. How do its profit-maximizing fare, quantity and economic profit change?
options: Fare rises to $78 and quantity stays at 30; economic profit is unchanged.
Fare and quantity stay at $72 and 30; economic profit is unchanged because MR has a gap.
Fare falls and quantity rises; economic profit falls by less than $180.
Fare and quantity stay at $72 and 30; economic profit falls by $180.
P62I-OLI-L-072.feedback: At Q=30 the MR gap runs from $36 to $60. Both MC=$48 and MC=$54 fall inside it, so the optimum remains at the kink, P=$72 and Q=30. Cost rises $6 on each of 30 units, lowering profit by $180.
P62I-OLI-L-072.imageAlt: Kinked demand at quantity 30, price 72, with two MR branches and MC at 48.
P62I-OLI-L-072.graphDescription: Quantity is horizontal and dollars per unit vertical. Demand follows P=84−0.4Q for Q up to 30, then P=108−1.2Q for larger Q. At Q=30, the upper MR branch ends at 60 and the lower branch begins at 36. MC is horizontal at 48.

P62I-OLI-L-073.q: A firm faces the kinked demand shown: P=70−0.5Q up to Q=20 and P=90−1.5Q above Q=20. Its constant MC initially equals $40. Compare a rise in MC to $45 with a rise to $55, holding demand fixed. Which conclusion is correct?
options: At MC=$45 the firm keeps Q=20 and P=$60; at MC=$55 it reduces output to Q=15 and raises price to $62.50.
At MC=$45 and MC=$55 the firm keeps Q=20 and P=$60 because any cost change lies inside the MR gap.
At MC=$45 the firm keeps Q=20 and P=$60; at MC=$55 it expands output to Q=25 and lowers price to $52.50.
At MC=$45 it reduces output to Q=15 and raises price to $62.50; at MC=$55 it returns to Q=20 and P=$60.
P62I-OLI-L-073.feedback: At the kink MR drops from $50 to $30. MC=$45 lies within that range, but MC=$55 lies above it. On the upper demand branch MR=70−Q, so 70−Q=55 gives Q=15 and P=70−0.5×15=$62.50.
P62I-OLI-L-073.imageAlt: Kinked demand at quantity 20, price 60, with two MR branches and MC at 40.
P62I-OLI-L-073.graphDescription: Quantity is horizontal and dollars per unit vertical. Demand follows P=70−0.5Q for Q up to 20, then P=90−1.5Q for larger Q. At Q=20, the upper MR branch ends at 50 and the lower branch begins at 30. MC is horizontal at 40.

P62I-OLI-L-074.q: A firm faces the kinked demand shown, with prevailing price $72, quantity 30 and constant MC=$48. options: Price and quantity stay at the kink; the $180 variable-cost saving exceeds the $300 fee, so economic profit rises by $120.
Price and quantity stay at the kink; the $180 variable-cost saving is smaller than the $300 fee, so economic profit falls by $120.
The fixed fee raises MC above the MR gap, so quantity falls; the variable-cost saving cannot affect profit.
The lower MC moves quantity above the kink; the fixed fee is a variable cost, so profit is unchanged.
P62I-OLI-L-074.feedback: The MR gap at Q=30 is $36 to $60; MC=$42 remains inside it, so P and Q stay at $72 and 30. Variable cost falls by ($48−$42)×30=$180. The $300 fixed fee does not enter MC but exceeds that saving, reducing profit by $120.

P62B-ELAS-LB-008.q: A seller sees no quantity response after a tiny price test. Why is concluding perfectly inelastic demand premature?
options: The zero response estimates elasticity precisely at zero; repeat the same tiny test only to check the seller’s revenue arithmetic.
The test may hide a response because of noise, contracts or its size; vary the test and allow adjustment before treating demand as perfectly inelastic.
The test establishes elastic demand because buyers delayed purchases; a larger increase must therefore raise revenue.
The test establishes unit elasticity because quantity was stable; the next test should hold total revenue constant.
P62B-ELAS-LB-008.feedback: Observed response may be imprecise or constrained over the test window.

P62B-ELAS-LB-018.q: A firm estimates the price elasticity of demand at 1.05, with a wide confidence interval spanning values below and above one. What is the prudent pricing conclusion?
options: The price increase should lower revenue because the point estimate exceeds one; the interval affects the size but cannot affect the sign.
The price increase should raise revenue because the interval includes inelastic values; the point estimate affects the size but cannot affect the sign.
Revenue should be unchanged because the interval includes one; averaging elastic and inelastic estimates guarantees unit elasticity.
The revenue effect of a small price change is uncertain because plausible elasticity values fall on both sides of one; use cautious testing.
P62B-ELAS-LB-018.feedback: Sampling uncertainty around one makes the revenue prediction ambiguous.

P62B-ELAS-LB-019.q: A product is a necessity but has many close generic substitutes. Which determinant should dominate brand-level demand?
options: Brand demand can be elastic even if category demand is inelastic, because consumers can switch brands without giving up the necessity.
Brand demand should be less elastic than category demand, because a brand includes fewer possible purchases than the category.
Brand and category demand should have equal elasticity, because both purchases satisfy the same basic need.
Brand demand can be elastic only if the entire category is a luxury, because generic substitutes cannot change necessity status.
P62B-ELAS-LB-019.feedback: Elasticity depends on the defined choice set.

P62B-ELAS-LB-020.q: A product has no close substitutes today but represents a large budget share. What is the best conclusion?
options: Few substitutes establish inelastic demand; budget share changes spending levels but cannot affect responsiveness.
Few substitutes restrain responsiveness while a large budget share encourages adjustment; estimate their combined effect in this market.
The large budget share establishes elastic demand; the absence of substitutes changes price but cannot affect responsiveness.
The two determinants imply unit elasticity; their opposing directions necessarily cancel quantitatively.
P62B-ELAS-LB-020.feedback: Elasticity determinants are tendencies, not mechanical rules.

P62B-ELAS-LB-022.q: A market’s supply is inelastic today but highly elastic over five years. A permanent tax is imposed. How should incidence analysis change over time?
options: If demand responsiveness is unchanged, the more elastic long-run supply tends to shift more of the burden to sellers.
If demand responsiveness is unchanged, supply adjustment raises the quantity traded but leaves the burden shares at their short-run values.
If demand responsiveness is unchanged, producers’ ability to adjust makes the statutory taxpayer bear a larger share over time.
If demand responsiveness is unchanged, the more elastic long-run supply tends to shift more of the burden to buyers.
P62B-ELAS-LB-022.feedback: Relative elasticities evolve as producers gain exit and adjustment options.

P62B-ELAS-LB-025.q: A seller estimates elastic demand but still raises price after a cost increase. Why is this not necessarily irrational?
options: Elastic demand predicts a revenue loss from a price rise, so profit must fall by the same amount even if the firm avoids variable costs.
Elastic demand predicts a revenue gain from a price rise, and that gain is sufficient to establish a profit gain after the cost increase.
Elastic demand predicts a revenue loss from a price rise, but reduced unit sales and higher contribution margins may improve profit after the cost increase.
Elastic demand predicts unchanged revenue from a price rise, so the cost increase can be passed on without checking the quantity response.
P62B-ELAS-LB-025.feedback: Revenue and profit are different objectives; cost pass-through depends on the full optimization problem.

P62B-ELAS-LB-035.q: A firm has customer-level elasticity estimates, capacity constraints, and rising marginal cost. Why is charging the lowest price to the most elastic customers not automatically optimal?
options: A lower price may attract more units from responsive customers, but those units use scarce capacity and may carry rising marginal cost; compare incremental contribution across feasible uses.
A lower price attracts more units from responsive customers, so allocate all capacity to them even when their incremental contribution is lower.
Rising marginal cost changes total profit but not the contribution of extra units, so allocate capacity using elasticity alone.
A capacity limit makes demand responses irrelevant until capacity expands, so allocate current capacity only by customers’ average spending.
P62B-ELAS-LB-035.feedback: Optimal pricing integrates demand response with costs and capacity.

P62E-COP-EL-028.q: A firm compares two technologies. Technology A has higher fixed cost and lower MC. Which statement is defensible without revenue information?
options: A has lower ATC at low output but higher ATC at high output; lower MC matters most when few units are produced.
A has lower ATC at every output; the lower MC offsets the fixed-cost difference by the same amount at every scale.
A has higher ATC at every output; the higher fixed cost increases the cost of each additional unit.
A may have lower ATC at high output but higher ATC at low output; the fixed-cost burden is spread as production expands.
P62E-COP-EL-028.feedback: The fixed-versus-variable tradeoff depends on output.

P62G-MON-EL-018.q: A patent increases expected innovation but also permits monopoly pricing under demand P = 110 − 2Q. Which evaluation is economically complete?
options: Compare expected innovation gains with the entire transfer from buyers to the patent holder, treating that transfer as lost total surplus.
Compare the patent holder’s additional profit with the static welfare loss, treating that profit as the full social value of innovation.
Compare expected innovation gains with production costs alone, excluding foregone gains on units priced out of the market.
Compare expected innovation gains with static welfare loss from output restriction, and assess the distribution of gains separately.
P62G-MON-EL-018.feedback: Patent policy trades static efficiency against innovation incentives.

P62G-MON-EL-021.q: A patent increases expected innovation but also permits monopoly pricing under demand P = 105 − 1.75Q. Which evaluation is economically complete?
options: Compare expected innovation gains with the entire transfer from buyers to the patent holder, treating that transfer as lost total surplus.

P62G-MON-EL-021.feedback: Patent policy trades static efficiency against innovation incentives.

P62I-OLI-EL-027.q: A merger creates a verifiable 20% marginal-cost reduction but removes the closest rival. Which analysis is strongest?
options: Compare the pricing incentive from weaker rivalry with the extent to which marginal-cost savings reach consumers.
Use the 20% marginal-cost reduction as a 20% predicted price reduction, then evaluate rivalry only if that prediction fails.
Use the lost rival to predict a price rise of its former market share, then subtract the cost reduction percentage.
Treat the lower marginal cost as a fixed-cost saving, so it affects profit but provides no possible offset to higher pricing incentives.
P62I-OLI-EL-027.feedback: Oligopoly policy requires evidence about conduct, entry, efficiencies, and consumer effects.

P62F-PC-EL-011.q: A firm initially earns profit. A fixed annual fee raises ATC above price but leaves price above AVC. What happens in the short run and long run?
options: Shut down in the short run because price is below ATC; reenter in the long run once variable cost has been recovered.
Continue in both periods because price covers AVC; an avoidable annual fee cannot affect the long-run decision.
Continue in the short run because price covers AVC; persistent losses can lead to exit when the annual fee can be avoided.
Increase output in the short run to spread the fee; remain in the long run if total revenue exceeds variable cost.
P62F-PC-EL-011.feedback: Fixed cost does not change short-run output, but persistent loss can cause exit.

P62F-PC-EL-013.q: A technology improvement lowers MC and AVC but not market price. Which sequence is correct?
options: At the existing price the firm expands output and profit tends to rise; subsequent entry can increase market supply and lower price.
At the existing price the firm contracts output and profit tends to rise; subsequent entry can reduce market supply and raise price.
At the existing price the firm expands output and profit tends to fall; subsequent exit can increase market supply and lower price.
At the existing price the firm leaves output unchanged because only ATC matters; subsequent entry raises price to cover costs.
P62F-PC-EL-013.feedback: Lower costs raise firm supply and profit, inviting entry.

P62F-PC-EL-030.q: The product is standardized and firms are small, but buyers have severe information problems. Which judgment is best?
options: Price-taking must fail because informed buyers are required even for a small firm to face a given market price.
Price-taking may still describe firms, while the welfare benchmark is weakened because informed choice is a separate requirement.
The standard welfare conclusion remains intact because standardization makes information irrelevant to consumer valuation.
Entry restores the standard welfare conclusion without changing information, because zero profit establishes efficient buyer choices.
P62F-PC-EL-030.feedback: Some assumptions can fit while others fail.

P62I-OLI-EL-004.q: Refer to the payoff matrix. How does the Nash equilibrium compare with the joint-payoff-maximizing outcome?
options: Nash equilibrium is (A,X), total payoff 20; joint payoff is maximized at (B,Y), total 14.
Nash equilibrium is (B,Y), total payoff 14; joint payoff is maximized at (A,X), total 20.
Nash equilibrium is (A,Y), total payoff 19; joint payoff is maximized at (A,X), total 20.
Nash equilibrium is (B,X), total payoff 19; joint payoff is maximized at (A,X), total 20.
P62I-OLI-EL-004.feedback: Against X, the row player prefers B (14 rather than 10); against Y it also prefers B (7 rather than 5). The column player prefers Y against either row. Thus (B,Y) is the unique mutual best response, although (A,X) has the highest combined payoff, 20.

P62I-OLI-EL-006.q: Refer to the payoff matrix. How does the Nash equilibrium compare with the joint-payoff-maximizing outcome?
options: Nash equilibrium is (A,X), total payoff 32; joint payoff is maximized at (B,Y), total 18.
Nash equilibrium is (A,Y), total payoff 27; joint payoff is maximized at (A,X), total 32.
Nash equilibrium is (B,X), total payoff 27; joint payoff is maximized at (A,X), total 32.
Nash equilibrium is (B,Y), total payoff 18; joint payoff is maximized at (A,X), total 32.
P62I-OLI-EL-006.feedback: Against X, the row player prefers B (21 rather than 16); against Y it also prefers B (9 rather than 6). The column player prefers Y against either row. Thus (B,Y) is the unique mutual best response, although (A,X) has the highest combined payoff, 32.

P62I-OLI-EL-010.q: Refer to the payoff matrix. How does the Nash equilibrium compare with the joint-payoff-maximizing outcome?
options: Nash equilibrium is (A,X), total payoff 20; joint payoff is maximized at (B,Y), total 16.
Nash equilibrium is (A,Y), total payoff 18; joint payoff is maximized at (A,X), total 20.
Nash equilibrium is (B,X), total payoff 18; joint payoff is maximized at (A,X), total 20.
Nash equilibrium is (B,Y), total payoff 16; joint payoff is maximized at (A,X), total 20.
P62I-OLI-EL-010.feedback: Against X, the row player prefers B (12 rather than 10); against Y it also prefers B (8 rather than 6). The column player prefers Y against either row. Thus (B,Y) is the unique mutual best response, although (A,X) has the highest combined payoff, 20.

P62I-OLI-LB-023.q: A cartel member could earn an extra $12 million this year by secretly expanding output. If detected, it loses future profit with a present value of $30 million; detection probability is 60%. If undetected, future profit is unchanged. Under risk neutrality, which comparison determines whether to deviate?
options: The expected punishment is $18 million; comply because it exceeds the current gain.
The expected punishment is $30 million; comply because the full punishment is certain.
The expected punishment is $18 million; deviate because a current gain outweighs a larger discounted expected loss.
The expected punishment is $12 million; compare it with the $12 million gain using the probability of escaping detection.
P62I-OLI-LB-023.feedback: The future loss is already a present value. Multiply it by detection probability: 0.6×$30 million=$18 million. Net expected gain from deviation is $-6 million, so compliance is preferred under the stated assumptions.

P62I-OLI-LB-026.q: A cartel member could earn an extra $18 million this year by secretly expanding output. If detected, it loses future profit with a present value of $40 million; detection probability is 25%. If undetected, future profit is unchanged. Under risk neutrality, which comparison determines whether to deviate?
options: The expected punishment is $40 million; comply because the full punishment exceeds the current gain.
The expected punishment is $10 million; comply because any possible punishment outweighs the gain.
The expected punishment is $30 million; compare it with the $18 million gain using the probability of escaping detection.
The expected punishment is $10 million; deviate because the current gain exceeds it.
P62I-OLI-LB-026.feedback: The future loss is already a present value. Multiply it by detection probability: 0.25×$40 million=$10 million. Net expected gain from deviation is $8 million, so deviation pays under the stated assumptions.

P62C-CPS-EL-011.q: Buyer value is $50, seller cost is $20, and price is $47. Which statement is correct?
options: Total surplus $30; buyer receives $27; seller receives $3.
Total surplus $50; buyer receives $3; seller receives $47.
Total surplus $30; buyer receives $3; seller receives $27.
Total surplus $47; buyer receives $3; seller receives $44.
P62C-CPS-EL-011.feedback: Total surplus is $50−$20=$30. The buyer receives $50−$47=$3, and the seller receives $47−$20=$27; the two shares add to $30.

P62C-CPS-EL-012.q: A buyer values a good at $50 and the seller's cost is $20. At a market price of $23, which statement is correct?
options: Total surplus $30; buyer receives $3; seller receives $27.
Total surplus $50; buyer receives $27; seller receives $23.
Total surplus $23; buyer receives $27; seller receives $-4.
Total surplus $30; buyer receives $27; seller receives $3.
P62C-CPS-EL-012.feedback: Total surplus is $50−$20=$30. The buyer receives $50−$23=$27, and the seller receives $23−$20=$3; the two shares add to $30.

P62F-PC-L-046.q: Demand rises permanently in a constant-cost industry. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: Short-run price and profit rise; entry raises firm costs, leaving long-run price above the original level.
Short-run price and profit rise; entry returns long-run price to the original level.
Short-run price and profit rise; entry lowers firm costs, leaving long-run price below the original level.
Short-run price and profit fall; exit returns long-run price to the original level.
P62F-PC-L-046.feedback: Short-run price and profit rise; entry returns long-run price to the original level. Free entry or exit eliminates persistent economic profit; the cost response to industry size determines the final price, not the original short-run price.

P62F-PC-L-047.q: Demand falls permanently in a constant-cost industry. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: Short-run price falls and losses appear; exit lowers firm costs, leaving long-run price below the original level.
Short-run price falls and losses appear; exit raises firm costs, leaving long-run price above the original level.
Short-run price falls and losses appear; exit returns long-run price to the original level.
Short-run price rises and profits appear; entry returns long-run price to the original level.
P62F-PC-L-047.feedback: Short-run price falls and losses appear; exit returns long-run price to the original level. Free entry or exit eliminates persistent economic profit; the cost response to industry size determines the final price, not the original short-run price.

P62F-PC-L-048.q: Demand rises in an increasing-cost industry. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: Entry lowers price from its short-run high, and unchanged input costs return the long-run price to the original level.
Entry lowers price from its short-run high, and external economies reduce the long-run price below the original level.
Exit raises price from its short-run low, and higher input costs leave the long-run price above the original level.
Entry lowers price from its short-run high, but higher input costs leave the new long-run price above the original level.
P62F-PC-L-048.feedback: Entry lowers price from its short-run high, but higher input costs leave the new long-run price above the original level. Free entry or exit eliminates persistent economic profit; the cost response to industry size determines the final price, not the original short-run price.

P62F-PC-L-049.q: Demand falls in an increasing-cost industry. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: Exit raises price from its short-run low, while lower input costs permit a long-run price below the original level.
Exit raises price from its short-run low, while unchanged input costs return long-run price to the original level.
Exit raises price from its short-run low, while lost external economies raise long-run price above the original level.
Entry lowers price from its short-run high, while lower input costs permit a long-run price below the original level.
P62F-PC-L-049.feedback: Exit raises price from its short-run low, while lower input costs permit a long-run price below the original level. Free entry or exit eliminates persistent economic profit; the cost response to industry size determines the final price, not the original short-run price.

P62F-PC-L-050.q: Demand rises in a decreasing-cost industry. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: Entry follows short-run profit, but scarce inputs raise costs and keep the new long-run price above the original price.
Entry follows short-run profit, and external economies can lower costs enough for the new long-run price to fall below the original price.
Entry follows short-run profit, and unchanged firm costs return the new long-run price to the original price.
Exit follows short-run losses, and external economies lower costs enough for the new long-run price to fall below the original price.
P62F-PC-L-050.feedback: Entry follows short-run profit, and external economies can lower costs enough for the new long-run price to fall below the original price. Free entry or exit eliminates persistent economic profit; the cost response to industry size determines the final price, not the original short-run price.

P62F-PC-L-051.q: Demand falls in a decreasing-cost industry. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: Exit releases scarce inputs, lowering firm costs and the new long-run price below the original price.
Exit changes market supply but leaves firm costs unchanged, returning price to its original level.
Exit can remove external economies, raising firm costs and the new long-run price above the original price.
Entry expands external economies, lowering firm costs and the new long-run price below the original price.
P62F-PC-L-051.feedback: Exit can remove external economies, raising firm costs and the new long-run price above the original price. Free entry or exit eliminates persistent economic profit; the cost response to industry size determines the final price, not the original short-run price.

P62F-PC-L-052.q: After a permanent demand increase, entry leaves input prices unchanged. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: With unchanged firm costs, the industry is increasing-cost and entry leaves price above the original long-run level.
With unchanged firm costs, the industry is decreasing-cost and entry pushes price below the original long-run level.
With unchanged firm costs, the industry is constant-cost but entry leaves price at the initial short-run peak.
With unchanged firm costs, the industry is constant-cost and entry returns price to the original long-run level.
P62F-PC-L-052.feedback: With unchanged firm costs, the industry is constant-cost and entry returns price to the original long-run level. Free entry or exit eliminates persistent economic profit; the cost response to industry size determines the final price, not the original short-run price.

P62F-PC-L-053.q: As firms enter after a demand increase, the price of specialized inputs rises. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: Rising specialized-input prices raise firm costs, so the industry is increasing-cost and long-run supply slopes upward.
Rising specialized-input prices lower firm costs by spreading fixed cost, so long-run supply slopes downward.
Rising specialized-input prices affect the number of firms but not their minimum ATC, so long-run supply is horizontal.
Rising specialized-input prices shift product demand right, so the long-run supply curve remains unchanged.
P62F-PC-L-053.feedback: Rising specialized-input prices raise firm costs, so the industry is increasing-cost and long-run supply slopes upward. Free entry or exit eliminates persistent economic profit; the cost response to industry size determines the final price, not the original short-run price.

P62F-PC-L-054.q: Industry expansion creates shared suppliers and cheaper logistics. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: Shared suppliers and cheaper logistics raise minimum ATC through competition for inputs, producing upward-sloping long-run supply.
Shared suppliers and cheaper logistics can lower firm costs as the industry expands, producing a downward-sloping long-run supply curve.
Shared suppliers and cheaper logistics lower market demand without changing firm costs, producing horizontal long-run supply.
Shared suppliers and cheaper logistics lower one firm’s price by choice while leaving industry costs and long-run supply unchanged.
P62F-PC-L-054.feedback: Shared suppliers and cheaper logistics can lower firm costs as the industry expands, producing a downward-sloping long-run supply curve. Free entry or exit eliminates persistent economic profit; the cost response to industry size determines the final price, not the original short-run price.

P62F-PC-L-055.q: Demand falls in a constant-cost industry and some firms leave. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: There are fewer firms, and survivors return to zero economic profit at a lower price because exit reduces their costs.
There are fewer firms, and survivors return to zero economic profit at a higher price because exit raises their costs.
There are fewer firms, and survivors return to zero economic profit at the original price because their costs are unchanged.
There are more firms, and survivors return to zero economic profit at the original price because demand has fallen.
P62F-PC-L-055.feedback: There are fewer firms, and survivors return to zero economic profit at the original price because their costs are unchanged. Free entry or exit eliminates persistent economic profit; the cost response to industry size determines the final price, not the original short-run price.

P62F-PC-L-057.q: After a demand decline causes exit, specialized input prices fall for surviving firms. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: Lower input prices shift surviving firms’ cost curves downward, so the new long-run price can be below the original price.
Lower input prices shift surviving firms’ cost curves upward, so the new long-run price can exceed the original price.
Lower input prices affect only demand, so surviving firms’ cost curves and long-run price are unchanged.
Lower input prices shift costs downward, but the long-run price must return to its original level despite the lower minimum ATC.
P62F-PC-L-057.feedback: Lower input prices shift surviving firms’ cost curves downward, so the new long-run price can be below the original price. Free entry or exit eliminates persistent economic profit; the cost response to industry size determines the final price, not the original short-run price.

P62F-PC-L-058.q: Entry following a demand increase bids up the price of a scarce industry input. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: The scarce input becomes more expensive, shifting firm costs downward and leaving the long-run price below its original level.
The scarce input becomes more expensive, shifting firm costs upward and leaving the long-run price above its original level.
The scarce input becomes more expensive, but entry changes only the number of firms, so long-run price returns to its original level.
The scarce input becomes more expensive, raising firm costs but lowering the new long-run price below its original level.
P62F-PC-L-058.feedback: The scarce input becomes more expensive, shifting firm costs upward and leaving the long-run price above its original level. Free entry or exit eliminates persistent economic profit; the cost response to industry size determines the final price, not the original short-run price.

P62F-PC-L-059.q: New suppliers and shared infrastructure appear as the industry expands after a demand increase. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: External economies shift firm costs upward; the industry requires a higher long-run price to support more output.
External economies shift market demand upward without changing firm costs; long-run price returns to its original level.
External economies shift firm costs downward; the industry can support more output at a lower long-run price.
External economies lower firm costs but require less industry output at a higher long-run price.
P62F-PC-L-059.feedback: External economies shift firm costs downward; the industry can support more output at a lower long-run price. Free entry or exit eliminates persistent economic profit; the cost response to industry size determines the final price, not the original short-run price.

P62F-PC-L-060.q: Industry contraction after a demand decline causes shared suppliers to disappear. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: Losing shared suppliers shifts firm costs downward, so the smaller industry can support a lower long-run price.
Losing shared suppliers affects market demand but leaves firm costs unchanged, so long-run price returns to its original level.
Losing shared suppliers raises firm costs but makes the smaller industry’s long-run price lower.
Losing shared suppliers shifts firm costs upward, so the smaller industry can require a higher long-run price.
P62F-PC-L-060.feedback: Losing shared suppliers shifts firm costs upward, so the smaller industry can require a higher long-run price. Free entry or exit eliminates persistent economic profit; the cost response to industry size determines the final price, not the original short-run price.

ECON-MG-FINALBOSS-4006.q: Before a tax, price is $20 and quantity is 1,000. Afterwards buyers pay $24, sellers receive $18 and 850 units trade. An analyst says the buyer burden is the entire tax and calculates revenue using the original quantity. Which correction is right?
options: The wedge is $6, buyers bear $4 per unit and sellers $2; revenue is $5,100.
The wedge is $4, buyers bear $4 per unit and sellers $0; revenue is $3,400.
The wedge is $6, buyers bear $4 per unit and sellers $2; revenue is $6,000.
The wedge is $6, buyers bear $6 per unit and sellers $0; revenue is $5,100.
ECON-MG-FINALBOSS-4006.feedback: The wedge is $24−$18=$6, split into the $4 buyer-price increase and $2 seller-receipt decrease. Only 850 units are taxed, so revenue is $6×850=$5,100.

ECON-MG-FINALBOSS-4008.q: A tax produces a $6 wedge and 850 sales, down from 1,000 without tax. A proposed increase would produce an $8 wedge and 600 sales. Which comparison correctly evaluates revenue and lost trades?
options: Revenue falls from $5,100 to $4,800 while lost trades increase from 150 to 400.
Revenue rises from $5,100 to $6,800 while lost trades remain 150.
Revenue falls from $6,000 to $4,800 while lost trades decrease from 400 to 150.
Revenue rises from $5,100 to $6,000 while lost trades increase from 150 to 400.
ECON-MG-FINALBOSS-4008.feedback: Revenue uses the quantity remaining under each tax: $6×850=$5,100 versus $8×600=$4,800. Relative to 1,000 untaxed trades, losses are 150 and 400. A higher rate does not guarantee more revenue.

ECON-MG-FINALBOSS-4017.q: An unregulated market trades 100 units. A binding ceiling makes sellers offer 60 units while buyers want 140; a tax instead produces 70 trades with buyers paying $12 and sellers receiving $9. Assume no evasion or government purchases. Which policy comparison follows?
options: The ceiling limits trades to 60 and leaves a shortage of 80; the tax permits 70 trades and raises $210.
The ceiling permits 140 trades and leaves a shortage of 80; the tax permits 70 trades and raises $210.
The ceiling limits trades to 60 and leaves a shortage of 40; the tax permits 70 trades and raises $300.
The ceiling limits trades to 100 and leaves a shortage of 40; the tax permits 70 trades and raises $210.
ECON-MG-FINALBOSS-4017.feedback: Ceiling trades are limited by the 60 units supplied, and shortage is 140−60=80. Under the tax, the $3 wedge on 70 actual trades yields $210. The two policies reduce trades by different mechanisms.

ECON-MG-LEGENDARYBOSS-9136.q: Untaxed price is $30. A $7 tax makes buyers pay $34 and sellers receive $27. Lawmakers propose collecting the same tax from buyers instead of sellers in the same competitive market, with unchanged demand, supply and enforcement. Which prediction correctly combines the observed burdens with the proposed change?
options: Buyers bear $4 and sellers $3 per unit; collecting from buyers shifts the full $7 burden to buyers.
Buyers bear $4 and sellers $3 per unit; changing the statutory payer alone does not change those economic burdens.
Buyers bear $3 and sellers $4 per unit; changing the statutory payer alone does not change those burdens.
Buyers bear $7 and sellers $0 per unit; collecting from sellers would reverse those burdens.
ECON-MG-LEGENDARYBOSS-9136.feedback: The buyer-price increase is $4 and seller-receipt decrease is $3, summing to $7. Moving collection between sides does not change the equilibrium wedge or relative responsiveness in the stated competitive setting.

ECON-MG-LEGENDARYBOSS-9137.q: In a competitive market, a per-unit tax initially raises buyer price, lowers seller receipts and reduces trades. Several years later suppliers can adjust output much more easily, while demand responsiveness is unchanged. Which statement correctly distinguishes the initial effect from the later burden comparison?
options: Initially buyers bear the full wedge; as supply becomes more elastic, sellers necessarily bear the full wedge.
Initially both sides bear part of the wedge; more elastic supply tends to move a larger share onto sellers.
Initially both sides bear part of the wedge; as supply becomes more elastic, a larger share tends to fall on buyers.
Initially seller receipts rise; later statutory collection determines which side bears the wedge.
ECON-MG-LEGENDARYBOSS-9137.feedback: The initial wedge separates a higher buyer price from a lower seller receipt. In the later comparison, suppliers have better adjustment options, so the relatively less responsive demand side tends to bear more of the tax.
