P62B-ELAS-LB-001.q: A price-comparison service makes close substitutes easier to find. Before its launch a 5% price increase reduced sales by 2%; afterwards the same increase reduces sales by 8%, over equal adjustment periods. Which interpretation and revenue prediction fit the evidence?
options: Absolute demand elasticity falls from 2.5 to 0.625; a small price increase now tends to raise revenue.
Demand becomes more elastic solely because the firm moves upward along an unchanged demand curve; comparison information plays no role.
Absolute demand elasticity rises from 0.4 to 1.6; a small price increase now tends to reduce revenue because buyers can switch more easily.
Demand remains inelastic because both tests use the same price increase; quantity responses cannot change the classification.
P62B-ELAS-LB-001.feedback: The response ratios are 2/5=0.4 and 8/5=1.6. Easier comparison improves substitution options. Above unit elasticity, the percentage quantity loss outweighs a small price increase.

P62B-ELAS-LB-003.q: A seller forecasts that a 5% price rise will raise revenue using today’s demand elasticity of 0.4. A close substitute launches before the planned price rise. Which revision and test would make the forecast more defensible?
options: Reestimate demand after entry; if elasticity rises above one, the predicted revenue effect can reverse.
Keep 0.4 because elasticity is a permanent property of the product; test only whether accounting costs changed.
Raise the revenue forecast automatically because a new substitute always increases demand for this seller’s product.
Use supply elasticity in place of demand elasticity because another producer has entered.
P62B-ELAS-LB-003.feedback: The new substitute changes buyers’ alternatives. The revenue prediction depends on responsiveness at the time of the price change, so an estimate above one can overturn the old inelastic-demand forecast.

P62B-ELAS-LB-007.q: Two customer groups buy the same product at the same price. A 4% price increase reduces Group A’s purchases by 2% and Group B’s by 8%. Both groups have the same adjustment period. B spends a larger income share on the product and has more substitutes. Which conclusion is justified?
options: A is less responsive than B, consistent with the stated budget-share and substitution differences; equal prices do not imply equal elasticities.
A is more responsive than B because a smaller quantity response gives the larger elasticity.
Both have the same elasticity because price and adjustment period are the same; the responses measure supply instead.
The comparison proves that time horizon explains the difference, despite the identical adjustment periods.
P62B-ELAS-LB-007.feedback: The absolute elasticities are 0.5 and 2. Greater budget exposure and more substitutes are plausible reasons for B’s stronger response; the equal time horizon rules out that particular explanation.

P62B-ELAS-LB-013.q: A national housing-supply estimate is 1.2 over ten years. City A has little buildable land and a one-year planning horizon; City B has available land and a ten-year horizon. Which use of the estimate is defensible?
options: Apply 1.2 to both cities because a national elasticity incorporates each local constraint equally.
Apply a larger elasticity to A because scarce land makes each price increase more valuable to owners.
Treat it as a starting point, not a common local forecast; A likely faces tighter short-run constraints, while B has more adjustment possibilities.
Apply zero elasticity to B because a longer horizon fixes the housing stock more tightly.
P62B-ELAS-LB-013.feedback: Supply responsiveness depends on available resources and adjustment time. A national long-horizon estimate cannot identify either city’s elasticity without local evidence, particularly A’s constrained short-run response.

P62B-ELAS-LB-024.q: A crop quota reduces sales from 1,000 to 900 units and raises price from $10 to $12. Farmers’ variable production cost falls by $300, while administering the quota uses $1,200 of their resources. Which comparison avoids confusing revenue with profit?
options: Revenue rises by $800 and profit must rise by $800 because the demand response is inelastic.
Revenue rises by $800, but net producer profit falls by $100 after cost savings and administration.
Revenue falls by $1,000 and profit falls by $1,900 because fewer units are sold.
Revenue rises by $1,200 and profit rises by $300 because use the old quantity at the new price.
P62B-ELAS-LB-024.feedback: Revenue changes from $10,000 to $10,800. Profit changes by +800+300−1,200=−$100. Inelastic response can raise revenue without making an administratively costly policy profitable.

P62B-ELAS-LB-026.q: A seller expects a small discount to increase revenue from customers with elastic demand. Those customers can freely resell purchases to customers currently paying the regular price. Which issue must the forecast address before treating the two groups’ sales as separate?
options: Resale guarantees the discount raises profit because every discounted sale is an additional market sale.
Resale makes both groups’ demand perfectly inelastic because the seller names two prices.
Resale affects fixed cost only, so it can be ignored when estimating demand responses.
Resale can shift regular-price purchases into the discounted channel; evaluate that switching as well as each group’s quantity response.
P62B-ELAS-LB-026.feedback: The elastic group may buy partly for resale, replacing rather than adding to regular-price sales. Separate response estimates do not by themselves establish the seller’s overall revenue or profit gain.

P62B-ELAS-LB-027.q: An importer initially cuts foreign-goods purchases by 2% when their domestic-currency price rises 5%. After close domestic substitutes appear, the same price increase cuts imports 9%. If foreign prices and currency needed per imported unit are unchanged, which implication follows?
options: Import demand becomes more elastic, so the derived quantity demand for foreign currency becomes more responsive to the same domestic-currency price change.
Import demand becomes less elastic because 9% is larger than 2%, so foreign-currency purchases become less responsive.
The foreign-currency quantity must rise when imports fall, because each imported unit now requires more foreign currency.
Derived demand is unchanged because domestic substitutes cannot affect purchases of foreign goods.
P62B-ELAS-LB-027.feedback: The import response ratio rises from 0.4 to 1.8. With unchanged foreign currency required per unit, a larger percentage fall in imports produces a larger fall in currency purchases.

P62B-ELAS-LB-028.q: A rival cuts its price 10%. Your product’s cross-price elasticity with that rival is +1.5, while your own-price elasticity is −0.5. Holding your price and other determinants fixed, which forecast and interpretation fit?
options: Your sales rise about 15%; positive cross-price elasticity means the goods are complements.
Your sales fall about 15%; the positive cross-price elasticity indicates substitutes.
Your sales rise about 5%; use own-price elasticity with the rival’s price cut.
Your sales fall about 0.15%; multiply by the elasticity as though it were already a percentage.
P62B-ELAS-LB-028.feedback: Use the cross-price coefficient for a rival’s price: 1.5×(−10%)=−15%. The positive relationship between rival price and own sales is the substitute pattern.

P62B-ELAS-LB-029.q: Income is forecast to rise 5%. Transit demand has income elasticity −0.6; leisure-rail demand has income elasticity +1.4. Prices and other determinants are fixed. Which forecast separates the sign from responsiveness?
options: Transit demand rises about 3%, while leisure-rail demand rises about 7%; discard the minus sign before forecasting.
Transit demand falls about 0.6%, while leisure-rail demand rises about 1.4%; coefficients are percentage changes themselves.
Transit demand falls about 3%, while leisure-rail demand rises about 7%; the estimates classify transit as inferior over this range.
Both demands rise 5% because the income shock is common to the two markets.
P62B-ELAS-LB-029.feedback: Multiply each coefficient by the 5% income rise: −0.6×5%=−3% and 1.4×5%=7%. For income elasticity, the sign identifies the direction and must be retained.

P62B-ELAS-LB-030.q: A producer’s price rises 8%. Its short-run supply elasticity is 0.25 and its long-run elasticity is 1.5, each applicable near the initial price. Which forecast and explanation fit, with other determinants held constant?
options: Quantity supplied rises 12% in the short run and 2% in the long run because time reduces adjustment options.
Quantity supplied rises 8% in both periods because elasticity measures the direction but not the size of the response.
Quantity supplied falls 2% then 12% because the higher output price raises the firm’s input costs by definition.
Quantity supplied rises about 2% in the short run and 12% in the long run as capacity and inputs can adjust.
P62B-ELAS-LB-030.feedback: Supply response is elasticity times the price change: 0.25×8%=2% and 1.5×8%=12%. Longer adjustment time can allow greater output response.

P62B-ELAS-LB-031.q: Two reports describe the same demand estimate as −2.3 and 2.3. A manager says they predict opposite sales responses to a 2% price increase. Which diagnosis is appropriate if the second report uses the absolute-value convention?
options: Both imply an approximate 4.6% sales decline; the second reports magnitude rather than an upward-sloping demand response.
One predicts a 4.6% decline and the other a 4.6% rise because absolute values reverse economic behavior.
Both predict a 2.3% sales decline because elasticity should not be multiplied by the price change.
Neither permits a revenue prediction because opposite printed signs prove the data disagree.
P62B-ELAS-LB-031.feedback: The signed estimate gives −2.3×2%=−4.6%. Reporting |Ed|=2.3 retains that downward-demand interpretation; it changes notation, not the estimated behavior.

P62B-ELAS-LB-033.q: A product has cross-price elasticity −0.9 with a companion service. The service price falls 10%. An analyst discards the minus sign and forecasts a 9% product-sales decline. Which correction is right?
options: Discard the sign: product sales fall about 9%, consistent with the purchases being substitutes.
Keep the sign: product sales fall about 0.9%, because the coefficient already contains the 10% price change.
Keep the sign: product sales rise about 9%, consistent with the two purchases being complements.
Discard both signs: product sales are unchanged because cross-price elasticity cannot predict quantity.
P62B-ELAS-LB-033.feedback: For cross-price elasticity the sign distinguishes complements from substitutes. (−0.9)×(−10%)=+9%, so a cheaper complement raises demand for the product.

P62B-ELAS-LB-034.q: A binding posted-price ceiling holds the seller’s receipt at $10. Buyers must also pay a $2 per-unit tax, and approved buyers receive a $1 per-unit subsidy. Supply at the ceiling is only 60 units while buyers seek 100. Which analysis correctly distinguishes prices from actual trades?
options: Approved buyers pay $9 and sellers receive $12; all 100 desired units trade because the subsidy removes scarcity.
Approved buyers pay $13 and sellers receive $10; trades are 100 because all policy amounts should be added to demand.
Approved buyers pay $11 and sellers receive $10; trades are necessarily 100 because those prices clear any market.
Approved buyers’ net monetary outlay is $11 and sellers receive $10; trades are limited to 60, so a demand-elasticity calculation alone cannot establish 100 sales.
P62B-ELAS-LB-034.feedback: For approved buyers, $10+$2−$1=$11. Sellers still receive the capped $10, at which only 60 units are supplied. The binding shortage constrains actual trades regardless of desired purchases.

P62B-ELAS-B3-004.q: A farm quota reduces quantity 5% and raises price 8%, with no other change. A student says fewer sales must lower revenue. Which correction is right using the exact stated percentage changes?
options: Revenue falls 5% because the price increase does not affect revenue per sale.
Revenue rises exactly 13% because the magnitudes of both percentage changes should be added.
Revenue stays unchanged because all quota policies imply unit elasticity.
Revenue rises about 2.6% because 1.08×0.95=1.026; quantity falls proportionately less than price rises.
P62B-ELAS-B3-004.feedback: Revenue is price times quantity. The new revenue factor is 1.08×0.95=1.026, so revenue rises 2.6%; a lower quantity alone does not determine revenue.

P62B-ELAS-B3-005.q: A seller faces downward-sloping demand with absolute elasticity 0.8 at its current output. An analyst proposes a small output expansion to raise total revenue. Which response follows from elasticity, without needing a cost model?
options: Reject the revenue claim: the current range is inelastic, so marginal revenue is negative and a small output reduction raises revenue.
Accept the claim: any positive price makes marginal revenue positive regardless of elasticity.
Reject the claim because marginal revenue is zero whenever elasticity is below one.
Accept the claim because inelastic demand means quantity changes proportionately more than price.
P62B-ELAS-B3-005.feedback: In the inelastic range, expanding sales requires a proportionately large price reduction, reducing revenue. Thus MR is negative; the conclusion is about revenue rather than a complete profit choice.

P62B-ELAS-B3-006.q: Demand is Q=120−3P. Compare P=$30 with P=$10. Which statement explains why a constant slope does not imply constant point elasticity?
options: Both points have |Ed|=3 because the demand slope is −3, so revenue falls at both.
At $30, Q=30 and |Ed|=3; at $10, Q=90 and |Ed|=1/3, so a small price rise lowers revenue at the first point but raises it at the second.
At $30, |Ed|=1/3; at $10, |Ed|=3, so revenue effects are reversed.
Both points have unit elasticity because the demand equation is linear.
P62B-ELAS-B3-006.feedback: Point elasticity is |dQ/dP|×P/Q. It equals 3×30/30=3 at the high price and 3×10/90=1/3 at the low price. The P/Q ratio changes even though slope does not.

P62B-ELAS-B3-007.q: Supply is Q=20+2P. At P=$20, a planner uses the slope 2 as elasticity and forecasts a 20% quantity rise after a small 10% price increase. Which correction is correct?
options: Elasticity is 2 because slope and elasticity are equal for any straight line; the 20% forecast is correct.
Elasticity is 60/20=3; the quantity response is approximately 30%.
Elasticity is 2×20/60≈0.67; the approximate quantity response is 6.7%, not 20%.
Elasticity is 0.67, so quantity falls 6.7% when price rises.
P62B-ELAS-B3-007.feedback: At P=20, Q=60. Elasticity multiplies slope by P/Q: 2×20/60=2/3. The forecast quantity response is (2/3)×10%≈6.7%.

P62B-ELAS-B3-009.q: A rival’s 10% price cut reduces a firm’s sales by 15%, with its own price held fixed. Using the resulting cross-price elasticity, what would a small 4% rival price increase predict, and what relationship is indicated?
options: About a 6% sales increase; the goods are substitutes because the cross-price elasticity is +1.5.
About a 6% sales decline; the goods are complements because the original sales change was negative.
About a 1.5% sales increase; elasticity is already a percentage forecast.
About a 2.7% sales increase; use the reciprocal of the observed response ratio.
P62B-ELAS-B3-009.feedback: The ratio is (−15%)/(−10%)=+1.5. A 4% rival-price rise predicts 1.5×4%=6% more sales, consistent with substitution.

P62B-ELAS-B3-010.q: Income falls 4% and product demand rises 6%, with prices and other determinants unchanged. If the estimated income elasticity applies to a subsequent small 2% income increase, what is the forecast and classification?
options: Demand rises about 3%; discard the negative sign when using income elasticity.
Demand falls about 3%; the good is inferior over the observed range.
Demand falls about 1.5%; the elasticity coefficient itself is the forecast percentage.
Demand rises about 8%; add the observed quantity change to the new income change.
P62B-ELAS-B3-010.feedback: Income elasticity is 6/(−4)=−1.5. Multiplying by the new +2% income change gives −3%. Its negative sign identifies an inferior good over this range.

P62B-ELAS-B3-012.q: A wage floor raises the wage employers pay by 10%. Estimated labor-demand elasticity is −1.4 in the short run and −2 in the long run. A forecast says employment must fall exactly 14% in both periods. Which correction follows under the stated fixed-demand-determinant estimates?
options: The approximate declines are 1.4% and 2%; elasticity coefficients already state total percentage changes.
Employment rises 14% and 20% because labor supply slopes upward.
Employment falls 14% in both periods because the same wage change implies the same quantity response.
The approximate declines are 14% and 20%; longer-run substitution makes the second response larger.
P62B-ELAS-B3-012.feedback: Multiply each elasticity by +10%: −14% and −20%. These are local approximations, not exact universal predictions, and different horizons need not share one elasticity.

P62B-ELAS-B3-019.q: Use the two labeled points on vertical D2. A student correctly computes zero midpoint demand elasticity, then concludes that total revenue is unchanged between the points. Which diagnosis is correct?
options: Zero quantity change gives zero elasticity, but the higher-price point has higher revenue because the same positive quantity sells at a higher price.
Zero elasticity also means zero price change, so equal revenue follows.
Zero elasticity means quantity rises enough to offset the price rise, so equal revenue follows.
A vertical demand curve has infinite elasticity, so the midpoint calculation must be reversed.
P62B-ELAS-B3-019.feedback: For vertical D2, quantity is unchanged while price differs. The midpoint quantity-change numerator is zero. Revenue is P×Q, so with a positive fixed Q the higher price produces higher revenue.

P62E-COP-LB-001.q: Northstar Bakery expects annual revenue of $186000, explicit costs of $118000, forgone salary of $42000, and forgone capital income of $12000. All comparisons use the same year and risk. A new outside job offers $61000; business revenue, explicit costs and the capital alternative are unchanged. Ignoring switching costs, which conclusion follows?
options: Accounting and economic profit both stay unchanged because no explicit business cost changed.
Accounting profit falls to $49000, but economic profit stays $14000; outside wages are explicit business costs.
Accounting profit stays $68000, but economic profit becomes −$5000; the outside alternative now pays $5000 more.
Accounting profit stays $68000 and economic profit rises by $19000; a better outside offer increases the business return.
P62E-COP-LB-001.feedback: Accounting profit is $186000−$118000=$68000. The new opportunity cost is $61000+$12000; subtracting it gives −$5000. Positive accounting profit does not establish that the business beats the best alternative.

P62E-COP-LB-004.q: Ironwood Furniture expects annual revenue of $242000, explicit costs of $151000, forgone salary of $53000, and forgone capital income of $18000. All comparisons use the same year and risk. For next year, revenue rises $20000, explicit costs rise $25000, and forgone capital income falls $10000; forgone salary is unchanged. Which comparison is correct?
options: Accounting and economic profit both fall $5000 because only explicit costs matter.
Accounting profit falls $5000, but economic profit rises $5000 to $25000.
Accounting profit rises $5000, while economic profit falls $5000 because capital income fell.
Accounting profit falls $15000 and economic profit falls $15000 because the lower outside return is an extra cost.
P62E-COP-LB-004.feedback: The business cash margin changes by +$20000−$25000=−$5000. The opportunity cost of capital falls $10000, so economic profit changes by −$5000+$10000=+$5000.

P62E-COP-LB-007.q: Harbor Roasters expects annual revenue of $164000, explicit costs of $97000, forgone salary of $38000, and forgone capital income of $9000. All comparisons use the same year and risk. A new technology would save $18000 in explicit costs but require owner capital that could earn an additional $25000 elsewhere. Revenue and forgone salary would not change. Which recommendation follows from the incremental comparison?
options: Retain the current technology: accounting profit would rise $18000, but economic profit would fall $7000.
Adopt the technology: accounting profit rises $18000, so economic profit must also rise $18000.
Adopt the technology: the additional $25000 forgone return is a benefit rather than a cost.
Retain the current technology because accounting profit would fall $7000 while economic profit rises.
P62E-COP-LB-007.feedback: Compare the $18000 explicit-cost saving with the $25000 added opportunity cost. The net economic change is −$7000, even though reported accounting profit would improve.

P62E-COP-LB-010.q: Cedar Trail Bikes expects annual revenue of $311000, explicit costs of $203000, forgone salary of $61000, and forgone capital income of $22000. All comparisons use the same year and risk. What outside salary would make the owner indifferent between continuing and the best alternative, and what happens if the offer is $3000 above that salary?
options: Indifference salary $108000; an offer $3000 higher leaves the forgone capital return irrelevant.
Indifference salary $61000; an offer $3000 higher leaves economic profit equal to the original $25000.
Indifference salary $311000; an offer $3000 higher changes accounting profit but not opportunity cost.
Indifference salary $86000; an offer $3000 higher makes economic profit −$3000 while accounting profit stays $108000.
P62E-COP-LB-010.feedback: Set revenue−explicit costs−salary−forgone capital return equal to zero: salary=$311000−$203000−$22000=$86000. A $3000 higher offer makes continuing $3000 worse than the alternative without altering business accounting profit.

P62G-MON-LB-003.q: Apex Water Authority has demand P=100−2Q, constant MC=$20, and an unavoidable fixed production cost of $200 over the comparison period. A regulator proposes marginal-cost pricing with a lump-sum subsidy to cover the fixed cost. Raising subsidy funds creates no additional distortion, but administration uses $50 of real resources. Compared with the unregulated monopoly, which welfare accounting is correct?
options: Output rises from 20 to 40; eliminating DWL adds $400, and net surplus rises $350 after administration.
Output rises from 20 to 40; subtract the $200 subsidy itself as a further resource loss, giving $150.
Output stays at 20; the subsidy covers fixed cost but cannot change a regulated output.
Output rises from 20 to 40; the entire $400 gain is a transfer to consumers, so net surplus falls $50.
P62G-MON-LB-003.feedback: MR=100−4Q gives Qm=20 and Pm=60. Demand=MC gives Qc=40; the recovered triangular gains are 0.5×20×40=$400. The subsidy is a transfer under the stated financing assumption; administration is a real incremental cost.

P62G-MON-LB-006.q: Beacon Patent Systems has demand P=104−2Q, constant MC=$20, and an unavoidable fixed production cost of $200 over the comparison period. Policy A caps price at $41, allowing quantity 31.5, with no administration cost. Policy B sets price at MC, allowing 42, but uses $466 of real administration resources. Any required financing is a nondistorting transfer. Which comparison of gains over monopoly is right?
options: A gains $110.25; B gains $441, so B is preferable because administration is a transfer.
A gains $330.75; B gains $466, so B is preferable because spending counts as a benefit.
A has no gain because it leaves some DWL; B gains $-25 and must therefore dominate A.
A gains $330.75; B loses $25 after administration, so A has the larger net surplus gain.
P62G-MON-LB-006.feedback: Original DWL is $441. At A, the remaining triangle is 0.5×10.5×21=$110.25, so A recovers $330.75. B recovers all $441 but uses $466, for −$25 net. Zero remaining DWL does not by itself identify the better policy.

P62G-MON-LB-009.q: Cobalt Rail Link has demand P=108−2Q, constant MC=$20, and an unavoidable fixed production cost of $200 over the comparison period. A lump-sum license charge of $100 is imposed with no output dependence or administrative resource cost. The firm remains active. Which comparison distinguishes tax revenue from monopoly DWL?
options: Q falls by 5, P rises, and DWL rises $100 because the license charge raises MC.
Q rises to 44 and DWL disappears because government receives part of monopoly profit.
Q stays 22, P stays $64, and DWL stays $484; profit falls $100, transferred to government.
Q and P stay unchanged, but DWL rises $100 because every profit reduction is lost social surplus.
P62G-MON-LB-009.feedback: A lump-sum charge does not change MR or MC, so the active firm keeps its original optimum. Its pre-charge profit is $768, sufficient to cover the charge. The $100 payment changes who receives surplus, not the output distortion.

P62G-MON-LB-012.q: Dune Mineral Trust has demand P=112−2Q, constant MC=$20, and an unavoidable fixed production cost of $200 over the comparison period. An innovation lowers MC to $10, with demand and fixed cost unchanged. A student says the lower monopoly price proves DWL must fall. Which calculation checks that claim?
options: Monopoly price falls from $66 to $61, so DWL necessarily falls by the same percentage as price.
Monopoly price falls from $66 to $61, but DWL rises from $529 to $650.25 because the efficient-output benchmark also expands.
Monopoly price rises from $66 to $61, and the efficient-output benchmark stays at 46.
Monopoly output rises to 51, eliminating DWL because lower MC makes monopoly pricing competitive.
P62G-MON-LB-012.feedback: After innovation Qm=(112−10)/4=25.5, Pm=61, and Qc=51. The new triangle is 0.5×25.5×51=$650.25, versus $529 originally. A lower monopoly price can coexist with a larger gap from the new efficient benchmark.

P62G-MON-LB-015.q: Evergreen Spectrum has demand P=116−2Q, constant MC=$20, and an unavoidable fixed production cost of $200 over the comparison period. Output stays at 24; the subsidy covers fixed cost but cannot change a regulated output.
Output rises from 24 to 48; the entire $576 gain is a transfer to consumers, so net surplus falls $70.
P62G-MON-LB-015.feedback: MR=116−4Q gives Qm=24 and Pm=68. Demand=MC gives Qc=48; the recovered triangular gains are 0.5×24×48=$576. The subsidy is a transfer under the stated financing assumption; administration is a real incremental cost.

Q stays 26, P stays $72, and DWL stays $676; profit falls $100, transferred to government.

P62G-MON-LB-024.q: Harbor Transit has demand P=128−2Q, constant MC=$20, and an unavoidable fixed production cost of $200 over the comparison period. An innovation lowers MC to $10, with demand and fixed cost unchanged. A student says the lower monopoly price proves DWL must fall. Which calculation checks that claim?
options: Monopoly price falls from $74 to $69, so DWL necessarily falls by the same percentage as price.
Monopoly price falls from $74 to $69, but DWL rises from $729 to $870.25 because the efficient-output benchmark also expands.
Monopoly price rises from $74 to $69, and the efficient-output benchmark stays at 54.

P62G-MON-LB-027.q: Ironwood Utility has demand P=132−2Q, constant MC=$20, and an unavoidable fixed production cost of $200 over the comparison period. A regulator proposes marginal-cost pricing with a lump-sum subsidy to cover the fixed cost. Raising subsidy funds creates no additional distortion, but administration uses $90 of real resources. options: Output rises from 28 to 56; eliminating DWL adds $784, and net surplus rises $694 after administration.
Output rises from 28 to 56; subtract the $200 subsidy itself as a further resource loss, giving $494.
Output stays at 28; the subsidy covers fixed cost but cannot change a regulated output.
Output rises from 28 to 56; the entire $784 gain is a transfer to consumers, so net surplus falls $90.
P62G-MON-LB-027.feedback: MR=132−4Q gives Qm=28 and Pm=76. Demand=MC gives Qc=56; the recovered triangular gains are 0.5×28×56=$784. The subsidy is a transfer under the stated financing assumption; administration is a real incremental cost.

P62G-MON-LB-030.q: Juniper Network has demand P=136−2Q, constant MC=$20, and an unavoidable fixed production cost of $200 over the comparison period. Policy A caps price at $49, allowing quantity 43.5, with no administration cost. Policy B sets price at MC, allowing 58, but uses $866 of real administration resources. Any required financing is a nondistorting transfer. Which comparison of gains over monopoly is right?
options: A gains $210.25; B gains $841, so B is preferable because administration is a transfer.
A gains $630.75; B gains $866, so B is preferable because spending counts as a benefit.
A has no gain because it leaves some DWL; B gains $-25 and must therefore dominate A.
A gains $630.75; B loses $25 after administration, so A has the larger net surplus gain.
P62G-MON-LB-030.feedback: Original DWL is $841. At A, the remaining triangle is 0.5×14.5×29=$210.25, so A recovers $630.75. B recovers all $841 but uses $866, for −$25 net. Zero remaining DWL does not by itself identify the better policy.

P62G-MON-LB-033.q: Keystone Licensing has demand P=140−2Q, constant MC=$20, and an unavoidable fixed production cost of $200 over the comparison period. A lump-sum license charge of $100 is imposed with no output dependence or administrative resource cost. The firm remains active. Which comparison distinguishes tax revenue from monopoly DWL?

Q rises to 60 and DWL disappears because government receives part of monopoly profit.
Q stays 30, P stays $80, and DWL stays $900; profit falls $100, transferred to government.
Q and P stay unchanged, but DWL rises $100 because every profit reduction is lost social surplus.
P62G-MON-LB-033.feedback: A lump-sum charge does not change MR or MC, so the active firm keeps its original optimum. Its pre-charge profit is $1600, sufficient to cover the charge. The $100 payment changes who receives surplus, not the output distortion.

Monopoly price falls from $82 to $77, but DWL rises from $961 to $1122.25 because the efficient-output benchmark also expands.

P62H-MCMP-LB-003.q: Keystone Café faces demand P=55−0.625Q and total cost TC=450+10Q+0.5Q². Its initial long-run optimum is Q=20, where P=ATC=$42.5; minimum ATC occurs at Q=30. A manager proposes producing 30 units solely to minimize ATC, selling them at the price on the same demand curve. Which diagnosis is correct?
options: At 30 units price is $36.25 and ATC is $40, creating a loss of $112.5; minimum ATC is not the profit-maximizing rule.
At 30 units price stays $42.5, so lower ATC guarantees a higher profit.
At 30 units price equals MC because that is where ATC is minimized, so the firm earns zero profit.
At 30 units demand shifts outward to cover costs automatically, eliminating the loss.
P62H-MCMP-LB-003.feedback: Use demand at the proposed output: P=55−0.625×30=$36.25. Minimum ATC is $40. Profit is (36.25−40)×30=$-112.5. The original MR=MC outcome can have excess capacity without being a mistaken firm choice.

P62H-MCMP-LB-006.q: Lantern Salon faces demand P=55−0.625Q and total cost TC=450+10Q+0.5Q². Its initial long-run optimum is Q=20, where P=ATC=$42.5; minimum ATC occurs at Q=30. An annual license fee adds $40 to fixed cost without changing demand or marginal cost. Which short-run and long-run sequence follows if the fee persists and exit is possible?
options: Short-run output falls because the fixed fee shifts MC upward; losses then encourage entry.
Short-run output rises to 30 to spread the fee; this alone restores zero profit.
Short-run output and profit stay unchanged because fixed cost never affects either short-run profit or long-run exit.
Short-run output stays 20 and profit falls to −$40; losses encourage exit, strengthening the remaining firms’ demand.
P62H-MCMP-LB-006.feedback: The fee leaves MR and MC unchanged, so the short-run optimum stays Q=20. Total profit falls dollar for dollar by $40. Persistent economic losses encourage exit; the surviving firms face fewer substitutes and stronger demand.

P62H-MCMP-LB-009.q: Meadow Fitness faces demand P=55−0.625Q and total cost TC=450+10Q+0.5Q². Its initial long-run optimum is Q=20, where P=ATC=$42.5; minimum ATC occurs at Q=30. A process improvement lowers variable cost by $3 per unit at every output. Demand is initially unchanged and other firms can eventually adopt the process. Which sequence correctly separates short-run adjustment from long-run entry?
options: MC falls; the firm initially contracts below 20 and raises price. Entry then restores its original positive profit.
Only fixed cost falls; output and price stay unchanged, and persistent profit cannot induce entry.
MC falls; the firm initially expands above 20 and lowers price, earning positive profit. Adoption and entry can later erode that profit without requiring P=MC.
MC falls; zero initial profit forces the firm to keep its old output and price until every other firm adopts.
P62H-MCMP-LB-009.feedback: New MC=7+Q while MR=55−1.25Q, giving Q=21.33 and P≈$41.67. At the old output alone, costs are already lower by $60, so profit opportunities arise. Entry/adoption can remove those gains, but zero profit is P=ATC, not necessarily P=MC.

P62H-MCMP-LB-012.q: Nimbus Apparel faces demand P=55−0.625Q and total cost TC=450+10Q+0.5Q². Its initial long-run optimum is Q=20, where P=ATC=$42.5; minimum ATC occurs at Q=30. A licensing reform reduces fixed cost to $112.5 and leaves MC unchanged. Entry then shifts each firm’s demand intercept until tangency restores zero profit; its demand slope stays 0.625. The new tangency is Q=10, P=ATC=$26.25, with minimum ATC at 15. Which interpretation reconciles the initial and final outcomes?
options: The lower fixed cost immediately shifts MC left, so the smaller final output must be a movement along the original demand curve.
Output need not fall immediately when fixed cost falls; the later entry-driven demand shift supports the smaller tangency output, while positive markup and excess capacity remain.
Zero long-run profit means price equals MC at 10, so the stated positive excess capacity proves the new outcome is impossible.
The new output must be 15 because entry makes every differentiated firm minimize ATC at its chosen output.
P62H-MCMP-LB-012.feedback: A fixed-cost reduction initially leaves MR=MC output unchanged and creates profit. Subsequent entry changes demand. At the new Q=10, MC=10+10=$20, below price $26.25; actual Q is also below 15. Thus zero profit can coexist with both markup and excess capacity after adjustment.

P62H-MCMP-LB-015.q: Oasis Bistro faces demand P=64−0.625Q and total cost TC=648+10Q+0.5Q². Its initial long-run optimum is Q=24, where P=ATC=$49; minimum ATC occurs at Q=36. P62F-PC-LB-013.q: Use the market and representative-firm panels. An analyst assigns the market’s total quantity to each firm and recommends producing at minimum ATC whenever that differs from the MR=MC quantity. Which correction preserves both the market-firm distinction and the operating decision?
options: Divide market price by the number of firms, assign market quantity to each firm, and use ATC alone to decide shutdown.
Take price from the market, but choose minimum ATC before considering MR; firms can then sell any desired amount at that cost.
Take price from the market, choose each operating firm’s output on rising MC at that price, and check AVC before production and ATC for profit.
Take the firm’s MC as the market demand curve, choose market quantity there, and ignore AVC if revenue is positive.
P62F-PC-LB-013.feedback: Market quantity is the sum of firms’ outputs, not the output of each firm. A price taker has MR=P; the candidate output satisfies rising MC=P when operating. AVC governs shutdown, while ATC determines economic profit.

P62F-PC-LB-014.q: Use the two-panel graph. A permanent demand increase raises market price before entry can occur. Assume a constant-cost industry with free entry. Which sequence correctly separates an incumbent’s immediate response from the final industry outcome?
options: Incumbents keep output fixed until entry occurs; the additional firms permanently maintain the initial price increase.
Incumbents expand by shifting their MC curves right solely because market price rises; entry then raises price further.
Incumbents choose a higher individual selling price than the market; entry later forces every firm to minimum AVC.
Incumbents expand along rising MC and may earn profit; entry then expands market supply until price returns to the original long-run level.
P62F-PC-LB-014.feedback: The initial higher market price raises each price taker’s MR, changing its output on the existing MC curve. Profit induces entry. With industry expansion leaving firm costs unchanged, long-run price returns to the original zero-profit level.

P62F-PC-LB-015.q: The graph initially shows P above ATC at Q1. An unavoidable fee for the current year raises fixed cost by more than the initial total profit, leaving demand, MC and AVC unchanged. The fee is avoidable by leaving before next year. Which sequence is correct?
options: Keep the same short-run output but incur a loss; if these conditions persist, exit can avoid the future fee.
Reduce short-run output because the fee raises MC; continue permanently because P still covers AVC.
Keep the same short-run output and profit because a fixed fee never affects profit.
Shut down immediately and avoid this year’s fee; reenter next year if P remains above AVC.
P62F-PC-LB-015.feedback: The fee does not change the MR=MC output or the current operating margin over variable cost. It does reduce profit, possibly below zero. A fee unavoidable now but avoidable next year separates short-run operation from long-run exit.

P62F-PC-LB-016.q: The graph shows AVC<P<ATC at the operating quantity Q1. Fixed cost is unavoidable this period. A student says shutting down removes the entire loss (ATC−P)Q1. Which comparison correctly evaluates production versus shutdown?
options: Producing incurs (ATC−P)Q1, while shutdown loses zero because all costs become avoidable immediately.
Producing incurs (ATC−P)Q1, while shutdown loses all fixed cost; producing covers (P−AVC)Q1 of that fixed cost and is preferable now.
Producing covers no fixed cost because P<ATC, so shutdown and production necessarily have identical losses.
Producing earns positive economic profit because P>AVC, so the stated loss rectangle should be ignored.
P62F-PC-LB-016.feedback: Revenue exceeds variable cost, so production contributes a positive amount toward unavoidable fixed cost. The operating loss is smaller than the fixed-cost loss under shutdown, although persistent losses can still lead to long-run exit.

P62F-PC-LB-017.q: The graph shows a firm below its AVC shutdown threshold. Compare an unconditional lump-sum grant with a per-unit subsidy large enough to raise the firm’s net receipt above that threshold. Fixed cost is unavoidable this period. Which operating comparison is correct?
options: Both policies change marginal receipts equally, so either grant necessarily restores production.
The lump-sum grant lowers MC and restores production, while the per-unit subsidy affects fixed cost only.
The lump-sum grant alone leaves the shutdown decision unchanged; the per-unit subsidy changes marginal receipts and can make production worthwhile.
Neither policy can change production because any firm with an initial loss must shut down forever.
P62F-PC-LB-017.feedback: An unconditional grant does not change the payoff difference between producing and not producing. A per-unit subsidy is earned only on output and changes the net price compared with MC and AVC, potentially crossing the operating threshold.

P62F-PC-LB-018.q: Use the short-run supply graph. Compare a rise in unavoidable fixed rent with a rise in the variable cost of every unit produced, holding market demand unchanged. Which statement separates the two effects on firm supply?
options: Both costs shift short-run supply upward by the same amount because both increase ATC.
The fixed rent shifts short-run supply upward, while higher variable cost affects only long-run exit.
Neither cost affects supply until entry occurs because a price-taking firm cannot change output.
The fixed rent alone leaves MC and AVC, and thus short-run supply, unchanged; higher variable cost can raise MC and the shutdown threshold.
P62F-PC-LB-018.feedback: The operating supply relation uses rising MC above minimum AVC. Fixed rent does not enter either marginal or variable cost, although it affects profit and later exit. Variable-cost changes directly affect the operating comparison.

P62F-PC-LB-030.q: At the current competitive output, price equals private MC=$18. Each extra unit also imposes $6 of uncompensated harm on others. A proposal uses a $6 per-unit tax instead of an output-independent license payment of equal expected revenue. Which comparison targets the external-cost distortion?
options: Both payments make MC=$24 because equal government revenue implies equal marginal incentives.
The lump-sum payment corrects the distortion, while a per-unit tax affects only the distribution of profit.
Neither payment can affect efficiency because P=private MC already guarantees a social optimum.
The per-unit tax makes the firm face the $24 social marginal cost at that output; the lump-sum payment does not change its marginal production incentive.
P62F-PC-LB-030.feedback: Social MC adds the $6 external harm to private MC. A per-unit tax places that harm in the private marginal decision; an output-independent payment changes profit without adding the same marginal incentive.

P62F-PC-LB-031.q: A price-taking firm initially produces at the minimum of ATC, where P=MC=ATC=$18, with no externalities. A temporary mandate forces it farther along rising MC to an output where ATC=$20 and MC=$23; market price stays $18. Which comparison is correct?
options: The original output is productively and allocatively efficient with zero economic profit; the mandated output is neither and creates an economic loss.
Both outputs are productively efficient because the original minimum ATC remains $18; the mandated output earns zero profit.
The mandated output is allocatively efficient because more output is produced, although ATC exceeds price.
The original output is inefficient because profit is zero; the mandated output improves efficiency by raising ATC.
P62F-PC-LB-031.feedback: Initially the chosen output actually attains minimum ATC and P=MC. Under the mandate, ATC is above its minimum and MC exceeds marginal value P; P<ATC also means a loss. A minimum somewhere on the curve is not enough to establish efficiency at another output.

P62C-CPS-L-001.q: 5 buyers each want one unit with values [50, 44, 38, 32, 26]; 5 sellers each can supply one with resource costs [45, 49, 53, 57, 61]. Values and costs are in dollars. Allocate goods to the highest values using the lowest costs. Which quantity maximizes total surplus, and what is that surplus?
options: 1 units; total surplus $5.
2 units; total surplus $0.
0 units; total surplus $0.
1 units; total surplus $50.
P62C-CPS-L-001.feedback: After ranking buyers and sellers, marginal gains are [5, -5, -15, -25, -35]. Sum the 1 positive gains for $5; another trade would lower total surplus.

P62C-CPS-L-002.q: 5 buyers each want one unit with values [28, 34, 40, 46, 52]; 5 sellers each can supply one with resource costs [45, 37, 53, 41, 49]. Values and costs are in dollars. Exactly 2 units are produced by the cheapest sellers, but the lowest-valued buyer receives one instead of the marginal buyer among the highest 2 values. What would reallocating that one unit, with no transaction cost, do?
options: Leave total surplus unchanged because output does not change.
Raise total surplus by $18 without changing output.
Lower total surplus by $18 because the original recipient loses the item.
Raise total surplus by $46 because the replaced buyer’s value is irrelevant.
P62C-CPS-L-002.feedback: The relevant buyer-value difference is $46−$28=$18. Production costs and quantity stay fixed, so that increase in use value is the change in total surplus.

P62C-CPS-L-003.q: 5 buyers each want one unit with values [54, 48, 42, 36, 30]; 5 sellers each can supply one with resource costs [14, 18, 22, 26, 30]. Values and costs are in dollars. After ranking values and costs, what is the largest quantity that maximizes total surplus, allowing trades with exactly zero marginal surplus?
options: 4 units; it is the largest maximizer because zero-gain trades are inefficient.
5 units; include the first negative-gain trade.
5 units; total surplus $100.
5 units; total surplus $130.
P62C-CPS-L-003.feedback: Marginal gains are [40, 30, 20, 10, 0]. 4 trades add positive surplus and the next adds zero. Both quantities tie, but 5 is the largest maximizing quantity.

P62C-CPS-L-004.q: 5 buyers each want one unit with values [32, 38, 44, 50, 56]; 5 sellers each can supply one with resource costs [39, 31, 47, 35, 43]. Values and costs are in dollars. A new handling requirement uses $8 of real resources for every completed trade, in addition to seller cost. What efficient quantity and total surplus follow?
options: 3 units and $45; handling is only a transfer between participants.
3 units and $37; subtract handling only once for the entire market.
2 units and $45; adjust quantity but leave the surplus sum unchanged.
2 units and $24; include handling in each marginal resource-cost comparison.
P62C-CPS-L-004.feedback: Subtract $8 from every marginal gain, yielding [17, 7, -3, -13, -23]. Only 2 remain positive; their sum is $24. Real per-trade resources can change both the cutoff and the welfare total.

P62C-CPS-L-005.q: 5 buyers each want one unit with values [50, 44, 38, 32, 26]; 5 sellers each can supply one with resource costs [15, 19, 23, 27, 31]. Values and costs are in dollars. The efficient allocation currently includes 4 trades. A new buyer could replace the next excluded buyer, with all other values and costs fixed. What minimum willingness to pay would make an additional unit create nonnegative surplus?
options: $31; compare the new buyer’s value with the next-lowest unused seller cost.
$26; the excluded buyer’s old value is the resource cost of adding a unit.
$27; use the cost of the last unit already supplied.
$80; an extra buyer must exceed all surplus already created.
P62C-CPS-L-005.feedback: The first 4 low-cost units are already used. The additional unit requires the next seller, at $31; a new buyer value equal to that cost gives zero incremental surplus, and a higher value gives a positive gain.
